source_text: Propterea igitur publici hostes Christiani, quia imperatoribus neque vanos neque mentientes neque temerarios honores dicant, quia verae religionis homines etiam solemnia eorum, conscientia potius quam lascivia celebrant. Grande videlicet officium, focos et toros in publicum educere, vicatim epulari, civitatem tabernae habitu abolefacere, vino lutum cogere catervatim cursitare ad injurias, ad impudentias, ad libidinis illecebras. Siccine exprimitur publicum gaudium per dedecus publicum? Haeccine solemnes dies principum decent, quae alios dies non decent? Qui observant disciplinam de Caesaris respectu, hi eam propter Caesarem deserent, et malorum morum licentia pietas erit, occasio luxuriae religio deputabitur? O nos merito damnandos! Cur enim vota et gaudia Caesarum casti et sobrii et probi expungimus? cur die laeto non laureis postes obumbramus nec lucernis diem infringimus? Honesta res est solemnitate publica exigente induere domui tuae habitum alicujus novi lupanaris. Velim tamen in hac quoque religione secundae majestatis, de qua in secundum sacrilegium convenimur Christiani, non celebrando vobiscum solemnia Caesarum, quo more celebrari nec modestia nec verecundia nec pudicitia permittunt, sed occasio voluptatis magis quam digna ratio persuasit, fidem et veritatem vestram demonstrare; ne forte et isthic deteriores Christianis deprehendantur, qui nos nolunt Romanos haberi, sed hostes principum Romanorum. Ipsos Quirites, ipsam vernaculam septem collium plebem convenio, an alicui Caesari suo parcat illa lingua Romana Testis est Tiberis, et scholae bestiarum. Jam si pectoribus ad translucendum quamdam specularem materiam natura obduxisset, cujus non praecordia insculpta apparerent novi ac novi Caesaris scenam congiario dividundo praesidentis? etiam illa hora qua acclamant: De nostris annis tibi Jupiter augeat annos. Haec Christianus tam enuntiare non novit, quam de novo Caesare optare. Sed vulgus, inquis. Ut vulgus, tamen Romani, nec ulli magis depostulatores Christianorum, quam vulgus. Plane caeteri ordines pro auctoritate religiosi ex fide; nihil hosticum de ipso senatu, de equite, de castris, de palatiis ipsis spirat. Unde Cassii, et Nigri et Albini? unde qui inter duas laurus obsident Caesarem? unde qui faucibus ejus exprimendis palaestricam exercent? unde qui armati palatium irrumpunt, omnibus Sigeriis atque Partheniis audaciores? De Romanis, nisi fallor, id est de non-Christianis. Atque adeo omnes illi sub ipsa usque impietatis eruptione et sacra faciebant pro salute Imperatoris, et genium ejus dejerabant, alii foris; alii intus, et utique publicorum hostium nomen Christianis dabant. Sed et qui nunc scelestarum partium socii aut plausores quotidie revelantur, post vindemiam parricidarum racematio superstes, quam recentissimis et ramossimis laureis postes praestruebant? quam elatissimis et clarissimis lucernis vestibula enubilabant? quam cultissimis et superbissimis toris forum sibi dividebant? non ut gaudia publica celebrarent, sed ut vota propria jam edicerent et in aliena solemnitate exemplum atque imaginem spei suae inaugurarent, nomen principis in corde mutantes. Eadem officia dependunt et qui astrologos et aruspices et augures et magos de Caesarum capite consultant, quas artes ut ab Angelis desertoribus proditas et a Deo interdictas ne suis quidem caussis adhibent Christiani. Cui autem opus est perscrutari super Caesaris salute, nisi a quo aliquid adversus illam cogitatur vel optatur, aut post illam speratur et sustinetur? Non enim ea mente de caris consulitur, qua de dominis. Aliter curiosa est sollicitudo sanguinis, aliter servitulis.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore Christians are public enemies because they do not give vain or false or reckless honors to emperors, because as men of true religion they celebrate their festivals with conscience rather than wantonness. For it is a great duty to bring hearths and marriage beds into public, to feast by neighborhoods, to abolish the city with the habit of a tavern, to force mud with wine, to run in crowds to insults, to shamelessness, to lust's allurements. Is public joy thus expressed through public shame? Are these festive days of princes fitting, which do not fit other days? Those who observe discipline out of respect for Caesar, these will desert it for Caesar, and the license of bad morals will be piety, and the occasion of luxury will be reckoned as religion? O we who are deservedly to be condemned! For why do we, chaste and sober and upright, expunge the vows and joys of Caesars? Why on a joyful day do we not shade the doorposts with laurels, nor break the day with lamps? It is an honorable thing, when a public festival demands it, to put on the habit of some new brothel for your house. But I wish, nevertheless, in this also, in the religion of secondary majesty, concerning which we Christians are accused of a second sacrilege, not to celebrate the festivals of Caesars with you, in the manner in which they are celebrated, which neither modesty nor reverence nor chastity permit, but because the occasion of pleasure rather than a worthy reason has persuaded, to demonstrate your faith and truth; lest perhaps even there they may be found worse than Christians, who do not want us to be considered Romans, but enemies of the Roman princes. I call to account the Quirites themselves, the very native plebeians of the seven hills, whether that Roman language spares any Caesar of theirs. The Tiber is a witness, and the schools of beasts. Now if nature had given a certain transparent material to hearts for seeing through, whose inner parts would not appear inscribed with the scene of a new Caesar, distributing a gift, presiding? And even in that hour when they acclaim: 'Jupiter, increase the years of our years for you.' This a Christian does not know how to utter, as much as to wish for a new Caesar. But the crowd, you say. As the crowd, yet Romans, and none more demanding of Christians than the crowd. Clearly the other orders, by authority, are religious from faith; nothing hostile is breathed by the senate itself, by the knights, by the camps, by the palaces themselves. Whence are the Cassii, and the Nigri, and the Albini? Whence those who besiege Caesar between the two laurels? Whence those who exercise the athletic art to squeeze his throat? Whence those who, armed, burst into the palace, bolder than all the Sigerii and Parthenii? From the Romans, if I am not mistaken, that is, from the non-Christians. And so all those, even under the very outbreak of impiety, and with a sacred face, used to make sacrifices for the salvation of the Emperor, and to worship his genius, some outside, others inside, and certainly gave the name of public enemies to Christians. But even those who now are revealed as associates or applauders of wicked parties, after the vintage of parricides, a surviving cluster, with how recent and branched laurels did they shade the doorposts? With how lofty and bright lamps did they cloud the vestibules? With how cultivated and proud couches did they divide the forum for themselves? Not so that they might celebrate public joys, but so that they might already proclaim their own vows and in a foreign festival inaugurate the example and image of their hope, changing the name of the prince in their heart. The same duties depend on those who consult astrologers and soothsayers and augurs and magicians about the head of Caesars, which arts, as betrayed by deserting Angels and forbidden by God, Christians do not use even for their own causes. For whom is it necessary to investigate concerning the salvation of Caesar, except by one who thinks or wishes something against it, or hopes and sustains something after it? For not with the same mind is consultation made about dear ones as about masters. Otherwise the care of blood is curious, otherwise the care of servants.

choices.why: Christians are seen as enemies of the state
emphasizing the authenticity of Christian faith
describing the immoral behavior of non-Christians

pass_b_english: Christians are public enemies for one reason: we refuse to offer emperors honors that are empty, false, or reckless. As people of true religion, we mark their festivals with conscience, not debauchery. What a 'great duty' the world calls it—dragging hearths and marriage beds into the street, feasting block by block, turning the city into a tavern, churning wine into mud, and sending crowds racing toward insult, shamelessness, and lust. Is public joy really expressed through public shame? Do these princely festivals deserve the name when they would disgrace any other day? Those who keep discipline only out of respect for Caesar will abandon it for Caesar; license will be renamed piety, and luxury rebranded as religion. Oh, we are rightly condemned! Why do we—chaste, sober, upright—erase the vows and joys of the Caesars? Why, on a day of rejoicing, do we not shade our doorposts with laurel or turn night into day with lamps? It is counted an honor, when the public festival demands it, to dress your house in the livery of a new brothel. Yet even in this second-tier religion—this 'religion of secondary majesty' for which we Christians are charged with a second sacrilege—I want to make a point by not celebrating the Caesars' festivals with you. The way you celebrate them violates modesty, reverence, and chastity; pleasure, not worthy reason, drives the show. Let your own faith and truth be proven by this; otherwise, you may be found worse than the Christians you refuse to call Romans, branding us instead as enemies of the Roman princes.

I call the Quirites themselves to account—the native plebeians of the seven hills: does the Roman tongue spare a single one of their Caesars? The Tiber testifies, and the beast-schools. If nature had given hearts a transparent window, whose inner chambers would not show the scene of a new Caesar presiding over a donative, freshly inscribed? Even in the hour they cry, 'Jupiter, add the years of our years to yours,' a Christian no more knows how to utter that prayer than to wish for a new Caesar. 'But the mob,' you say. The mob, yes—but Roman. And no one demands Christian blood more loudly than the mob. The other orders, by their authority, are religious from faith; the senate, the knights, the camps, the palaces themselves breathe nothing hostile. Where did the Cassii, the Nigri, the Albini come from? Who besieged Caesar between the two laurels? Who practiced the wrestler's art on his throat? Who, armed, stormed the palace, bolder than all the Sigerii and Parthenii? From Romans, if I am not mistaken—that is, from non-Christians. And yet, even at the very eruption of impiety, all those men performed sacrifices for the Emperor's salvation and worshipped his genius, some outside, some in, while pinning the label 'public enemies' on Christians.

Even now, those exposed as allies or cheerleaders of murderous factions—the surviving cluster after the vintage of parricides—with what fresh, branching laurels did they shade their doorposts? With what lofty, blazing lamps did they smoke their vestibules? With what plush, proud couches did they carve up the forum for themselves? Not to celebrate public joy, but to declare their private vows early and, in another's festival, inaugurate the image of their own hope, swapping the prince's name in their hearts. The same complicity clings to those who consult astrologers, soothsayers, augurs, and magicians about the Caesars' heads—arts betrayed by deserting angels and forbidden by God, which Christians will not use even for their own causes. Who needs to investigate the Emperor's safety except someone plotting against it, wishing it harm, or hoping to profit from his fall? You do not consult about loved ones the way you consult about masters; the anxiety of blood is one thing, the anxiety of slaves another.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the rhetorical questions and the distinction between the 'care of blood' (family) and 'care of servants' (masters). Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Locked Latin. All clauses, including the specific lists of names (Cassii, Nigri, Albini) and the description of the 'surviving cluster' (racematio superstes), are preserved.

The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving the meaning, structure, and key terms. The citations and theological arguments are consistent with the source. The title 'Christians and Public Festivals' appropriately captures the central theme. No errors in source identity, completeness, or doctrinal accuracy were found.
